note: Base-rate reference data for relationship/marriage outcomes, US-focused. Every baseline and factor below is cited to a specific named study, researcher, or institution — not a vague general list. Where the underlying research is genuinely mixed, or a commonly-repeated figure isn't traceable to one clean current dataset, that's said explicitly rather than presented with false precision. A factor that was carried over from an earlier version without being independently re-verified in the most recent research pass is marked as such. Treat all of this as planning base rates, not precise truths. The reasoning model uses these as grounding, not as a lookup table.

first_marriage_ending_in_divorce_estimat.note: The divorce rate has been declining for decades; older, still widely-repeated figures (43-50%) overstate the risk for recent marriage cohorts. ~40% is the current best estimate for marriages formed today.
first_marriage_ending_in_divorce_estimat.source: Institute for Family Studies, "Divorce in Decline: About 40% of Today's Marriages Will End in Divorce" (analysis of CDC/NCHS and Census data)

first_marriage_reaching_20yr_college_edu.note: Specific to college-educated women first married 2006-2010. Non-college-educated and male-specific figures differ and were not separately confirmed this pass.
first_marriage_reaching_20yr_college_edu.source: Pew Research Center, "8 facts about divorce, marriage and remarriage in the United States" (Oct 2025), citing Census Bureau data

first_marriage_reaching_20yr_general_pop.note: Rough population-wide estimate synthesized from Pew/Census reporting (roughly half of first marriages reach the 20-year mark). Less precisely sourced than the college-educated-women figure above — treat as directional.
first_marriage_reaching_20yr_general_pop.source: Pew Research Center reporting, general synthesis

cohabiting_couples_still_together_5yr.note: 51% of premarital cohabitations are still intact (cohabiting or since married) after 5 years; 49% break up.
cohabiting_couples_still_together_5yr.source: CDC/NCHS, National Survey of Family Growth

second_marriage_ending_in_divorce.note: A widely-repeated figure (commonly cited in a 60-67% range), but this pass could not trace it to a single current, official government dataset. Treat as a soft, commonly-cited estimate, not a precise confirmed number.
second_marriage_ending_in_divorce.source: Multiple secondary family-law and family-research sources; no single confirmed primary dataset identified

dating_relationship_breakup_hazard_under.note: Breakup hazard rate exceeding 60% within a given year for unmarried couples together less than a year — i.e. the probability of splitting up during that year, from a nationally representative panel. Most attrition in new relationships happens early.
dating_relationship_breakup_hazard_under.source: Stanford How Couples Meet and Stay Together (HCMST) project, Michael J. Rosenfeld et al.

factors.note: 5-year divorce risk: ~38% for teen marriages, ~27% for early-20s marriages — the strongest and best-quantified risk factor found this pass.
factors.source: Nicholas H. Wolfinger (Institute for Family Studies), analysis of National Survey of Family Growth data — the "Goldilocks theory of marriage"

factors.note: Lowest 5-year divorce risk (~10-14%) is for marrying between ages 25-34, with the optimum around 28-32; each year of age reduces divorce odds by roughly 11% up to about 32.
factors.source: Wolfinger / Institute for Family Studies, as above

factors.note: Divorce risk ticks back up after the early-30s optimum (~17% 5-year risk at 35+, for marriages formed since 1998) — later is not simply always better. This nuance corrects a common oversimplification.
factors.source: Wolfinger / Institute for Family Studies, as above

factors.note: Carried over from an earlier version of this file; directionally consistent with general demography literature on age-heterogamy, but not independently re-verified with a fresh citation in this pass.

Carried over from an earlier version of this file; directionally consistent with the college-educated-women 20-year survival figure above, but not independently re-verified as a standalone factor this pass.
Remarriages dissolve at higher rates than first marriages — see second_marriage_ending_in_divorce baseline and its caveat above.

Marriages where the couple moved in together BEFORE getting engaged were about 48% more likely to end than marriages where cohabitation started after engagement or marriage. This is a live, debated research area — some earlier work (Manning & Cohen) found the cohabitation effect fading for marriages since the mid-1990s, but the most recent large study finds it persists specifically for pre-engagement cohabitation.
factors.source: Scott Stanley & Galena Rhoades, "What's the Plan? Cohabitation, Engagement, and Divorce" (Institute for Family Studies, 2023)

factors.note: Arguing about money — especially early in the relationship — was found to be THE top predictor of divorce in this dataset, ahead of arguments about children, sex, or in-laws, and independent of the couple's actual income, debt, or net worth.
factors.source: Sonya Britt et al. (Kansas State University), "Examining the Relationship Between Financial Issues and Divorce" (Family Relations journal), longitudinal data from 4,500+ couples, National Survey of Families and Households

factors.note: Contempt (sarcasm, mockery, eye-rolling, sneering, hostile humor, name-calling) is the single strongest predictor of divorce identified in this body of research — part of the "Four Horsemen" framework, which predicted divorce with over 90% accuracy in the underlying studies.
factors.source: John Gottman, University of Washington "Love Lab" (3,000+ couples observed over four decades)

factors.note: In a 16-year longitudinal study of 373 couples, one partner's early disapproval of the other's friendships predicted divorce up to 15 years later, even after controlling for first-year marital quality and income. General social-network approval is a separately-documented protective factor.
factors.source: Longitudinal study published in Journal of Social and Personal Relationships

factors.note: Shared, mutually-approved social networks are a documented protective factor for relationship quality — the flip side of the friend-disapproval factor above.
factors.source: Same body of research as partner_disapproves_of_your_friends

mirror_stats: The current best estimate is that about 40% of marriages formed today will end in divorce — down from the 50% figure that's still widely (and inaccurately) repeated.
The single strongest predictor of divorce isn't conflict itself — it's contempt: sarcasm, eye-rolling, mockery. Gottman's lab predicted divorce with over 90% accuracy just from watching for it.
Money, not children or in-laws, is the single biggest predictor of divorce — and it holds regardless of how much a couple actually has.
The lowest divorce risk isn't for marrying as late as possible — it's a window, roughly ages 28 to 32. Risk creeps back up again after the mid-30s.
Couples who move in together before getting engaged see meaningfully higher breakup rates than those who wait until after engagement — timing matters more than living together itself.
Most relationship attrition happens early: in nationally representative data, unmarried couples together less than a year had a same-year breakup rate above 60%.
